findings.suggestion: Fix the document, not the code: the 400-vs-422 split is pinned elsewhere in the contract and the blind test branch reached the same reading (Fixtures.UNPARSEABLE_OUT_OF_RANGE_NUMERIC_URL, "No host from URI: 400"). Replace the `999.999.999.999` / empty-label examples in the 422 paragraph with `4294967296`, and say explicitly that out-of-range forms URI cannot parse remain 400.
findings.summary: openapi.yaml lines 79-82 ("Host policy and equivalent forms") and the 422 description at line 704 name `999.999.999.999` and "an empty label" as hosts that "cannot be canonicalised unambiguously" and are "refused with 422 url_rejected, never accepted and never downgraded to 400". They are in fact 400 invalid_request: java.net.URI.getHost() returns null for `http://999.999.999.999/`, `http://a..b/` and `http://1.2.3.4.5/` (verified on the same JDK 21.0.12 the pom targets), so parseOrThrow refuses them before requireShortenable/HostNormalizer ever runs. The spec contradicts itself - lines 98-101 say forms URI cannot parse a host from stay 400 - and the code follows the second sentence. Only hosts URI does parse and the normaliser then rejects (e.g. `http://4294967296/`) actually reach 422; that path works.

findings.suggestion: Either document the exception - "405 and 415 carry the framework's default body and are not part of the ApiError catalogue" - or add handlers mapping them onto ApiError (which needs a new catalogue entry, so it is a contract change). Recommend documenting, since the closed catalogue has no code that means "method not allowed".
findings.summary: openapi.yaml line 121 states "Every non-2xx response has the ApiError shape" and the catalogue is closed, but there is no handler for HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException, HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException or a generic Exception. The 405 the spec explicitly requires on the two new exempt paths (lines 58-61) therefore carries Spring's BasicErrorController body - {"timestamp":...,"status":405,"error":"Method Not Allowed","path":"/api/v1/customers"} - not ApiError. Same for 415 on a wrong Content-Type and 500 on anything unhandled. Newly consequential because 405 on /api/v1/customers and /api/v1/public/links is now reachable with no credentials at all, and the default body echoes the request path.

findings.suggestion: Add one sentence to the "Three surfaces" section recording that OPTIONS on the exempt paths answers 200 with an Allow header, or set spring.mvc.dispatch-options-request=false if the intent was 405 for every non-POST verb. Decide it rather than leave it to the default.
findings.summary: openapi.yaml lines 57-61 say the exemption is not method-aware and that non-POST verbs on /api/v1/customers and /api/v1/public/links "must reach Spring's dispatcher and answer 405". OPTIONS is not one of the four verbs listed and, with Spring MVC's default dispatchOptionsRequest=true, an unauthenticated `OPTIONS /api/v1/customers` answers 200 with `Allow: POST,OPTIONS` rather than 405 - undocumented behaviour on a path that is outside the session filter (the same request against /api/v1/links is 401, so the two new paths behave differently). Confidence is medium because this rests on a framework default rather than on code in this diff.

findings.suggestion: Either renumber so the nullable relaxation runs first, as the contract states, or amend note 7 to record the order actually shipped and why. The human on the migration diff needs the two to agree.
findings.summary: openapi.yaml note 7 (lines 249-252) pins the order of the two schema changes: "relax links.customer_id to nullable, and add a unique index over lower(email)", in that order. The implementation ships them the other way round - V3 is the unique index, V4 is the nullable relaxation. Note 7 also warns that the lower(email) index fails to apply where duplicates exist; on the shipped order that failure aborts Flyway before customer_id is relaxed, so a partially-migrated database is one where the anonymous-create path's column constraint is still NOT NULL. The 409 account_unavailable contract depends on the V3 index existing, so the dependency itself is satisfied.

findings.suggestion: Truncate to ChronoUnit.MICROS in LinkService as SignUpService already does, so the created-response value is the value that is stored and read back.
findings.summary: Timestamp precision is inconsistent across responses for the same resource. SignUpService truncates to microseconds (SignUpService.java:57) so the body matches what the TIMESTAMP(6) column will return, but LinkService.create/createAnonymous use a raw Instant.now(), so the 201 body carries nanosecond precision (e.g. ...T12:00:00.123456789Z) while a later GET /api/v1/links/{code} returns the rounded stored value (...123457Z). Both are valid ISO-8601 instants per openapi.yaml line 152, so this is not a schema break, but createdAt/expiresAt for one link differ between the create response and every subsequent read.

not_examined: Nothing was executed: no build, no integration run, no live request. Every status above is inferred from source plus one standalone compile of HostNormalizer, so framework-default behaviours (405/415 bodies, OPTIONS handling, Jackson's ISO-8601 instant rendering) are read, not observed.
POST /api/v1/sessions: the token itself - claims, issuer, the 24-hour expiresAt value in SignInResponse, and Bearer tokenType - was not traced into JwtIssuer/JwtVerifier.

The 429 path end to end: I read RateLimitGuard, the Retry-After flooring and the bucket-to-capacity mapping, but not redis/token_bucket.lua, so the retry-millis value feeding Retry-After is unverified.

GET /api/v1/links paging: the 400 boundaries (page<0, size 1..100) were read in the controller, but the LinkPage totals, the createdAt-desc/code-asc ordering and its stability across pages were not exercised.
POST /api/v1/links/{code}/abuse-reports error paths: the 400 for a reason over 500 characters and the 429 body were not traced; only the 202 path and the anonymous-link takedown were read.
clickCount exactness (durable total plus un-flushed Redis delta) and the ClickFlushJob interaction with the value reported by GET /api/v1/links/{code}.

The seeded fixtures the contract freezes: the V1/V2 migrations, the two seeded accounts' Argon2id hashes and the threat-denylist seed rows were not opened, so "alice@example.com signs in after the lower(email) index lands" is unverified.

Undocumented surfaces the spec never mentions: the actuator endpoints exposed in application.yml (health, info, metrics, prometheus) sit outside the session filter and were not compared against the contract, since the spec declares no operations for them.
Whether a request to an exempt path with an odd encoding (trailing slash, %2e, matrix parameters) still matches the exact-equality exemption - a routing/security question I left to that lens.
summary: The implementation honours the contract on every documented status, body and header I was able to check by reading, including the parts most likely to drift. The three 1.1.0 additions are faithful: POST /api/v1/customers is 201 with {customerId,email,createdAt} and no Location and no token, with 409 account_unavailable decided by the lower(email) unique index rather than a read-then-write; POST /api/v1/public/links is 201 with the narrower AnonymousLinkResponse (no status, no clickCount), no Location, owner column NULL, the anonymous TTL applied server-side, and a separate CreateAnonymousLinkRequest record so that alias/expiresAt are 400 under fail-on-unknown-properties rather than silently accepted; both paths are exempted from the session filter by exact string equality, not by prefix, and both charge their own IP-keyed bucket. The click path still returns 302 (not 301) with Location verbatim plus the pinned no-store/Pragma/Expires trio on redirect, 404 and 429 alike, and the single not_found body is a shared constant so it is byte-identical everywhere. Error bodies come from one closed ErrorCode catalogue with fields omitted unless invalid_request, and Retry-After is floored at 1 second. The equivalent-form work is genuinely shared: I compiled HostNormalizer and confirmed the spec's worked cases (2130706433, 0x7f000001, 017700000001, 0177.0.0.1, 012.0.0.1, trailing dot, IPv6 mapped, five-part names) all canonicalise as documented, and both UrlValidator and DenylistThreatCheck decide on its output. The most consequential divergence is documentary rather than behavioural: the spec's own examples of a host that "cannot be canonicalised" - 999.999.999.999 and a..b - are 400, not the 422 the document twice promises, because java.net.URI extracts no host from them and the syntax gate fires first (API-1); the document contradicts itself on this and the code follows the other sentence, so I would change the document. Beyond that, the undeclared verbs the contract deliberately leaves at 405 answer with Spring's default error body rather than ApiError, contradicting "every non-2xx has the ApiError shape" (API-2), and OPTIONS on the two new unauthenticated paths answers 200 rather than 405 by framework default (API-3). Nothing here is a break a caller could be harmed by today; all five findings are decisions somebody should take explicitly rather than inherit.
